summary: Business Development Companies (BDCs) are closed-end funds created by Congress in 1980 to invest in small and distressed U.S. companies. They offer high dividend yields and are accessible to retail investors, but carry high risks including interest-rate sensitivity and potential loss magnification. BDCs must invest at least 70% of assets in eligible companies and distribute at least 90% of income to avoid corporate taxes.

claims.text: Business Development Companies (BDCs) are investment vehicles that provide funding to small, medium-sized, and financially distressed companies.
claims.evidence_quote: Business Development Companies (BDCs) are investment vehicles that provide funding to small, medium-sized, and financially distressed companies, aiming to help them grow and regain financial stability.

claims.text: BDCs are publicly traded on major stock exchanges, allowing retail investors to invest in small growth companies.
claims.evidence_quote: BDCs are publicly traded on major stock exchanges, providing retail investors with an opportunity to invest in small growth companies, unlike venture capital funds that primarily cater to large institutions and wealthy individuals.

claims.text: To qualify as a BDC, a company must invest at least 70% of its assets in U.S. firms with market values under $250 million.
claims.evidence_quote: To qualify as a BDC, a company must invest at least 70% of its assets in U.S. firms with market values under $250 million and offer managerial assistance to these businesses, as per the Investment Company Act of 1940.

claims.text: BDCs avoid corporate income taxes by distributing at least 90% of their income to shareholders.
claims.evidence_quote: Business development companies avoid corporate income taxes by distributing at least 90% of their income to shareholders.

claims.text: BDCs are similar to venture capital funds but allow smaller, non-accredited investors to participate.
claims.evidence_quote: BDCs allow smaller, non-accredited investors to invest in them, and by extension, in small growth companies.

claims.text: BDCs are sensitive to interest-rate spikes, which can impede profit margins.
claims.evidence_quote: A rise in interest rates—making it more expensive to borrow funds—can impede a BDC’s profit margins.

claims.text: BDCs often employ leverage, which can magnify losses.
claims.evidence_quote: Losses can be magnified because BDCs often employ leverage—that is, they borrow the money they invest or loan to their target companies.

claims.text: Dividends from BDCs are taxed as ordinary income because they don't meet the criteria for qualified dividends.
claims.evidence_quote: Dividends from BDCs are taxed as income because they don’t meet the criteria for qualified dividends.

claims.text: BDCs can make money by purchasing equity, converting bonds, or lending capital.
claims.evidence_quote: BDCs make money by lending capital to and purchasing equity or bonds from the companies in their portfolio.

claims.text: BDCs were created by Congress in 1980 to help small businesses grow while shielding them from predatory tactics.
claims.evidence_quote: They were created by Congress in 1980 to help small businesses grow while attempting to shield them from predatory tactics sometimes used to take over struggling businesses.
